etymology: Hebrew Makir, “sold” or “bartered,” a man of Lo-debar east of Jordan; not to be confused with Machir the son of Manasseh.
biblical_def: Machir the son of Ammiel was a wealthy man of Lo-debar, east of the Jordan, remembered for two acts of kindness toward the house and person of David. It was in the house of Machir that Mephibosheth, the lame son of Jonathan, found shelter after the fall of Saul’s house, until David sought him out to show him kindness for Jonathan’s sake (2Sa 9:4–5). Later, when David fled from Absalom and came weary and hungry to Mahanaim, Machir was one of three men — with Shobi and Barzillai — who brought beds and basons and earthen vessels, wheat and barley, honey and butter and cheese, for the king and the people that were with him (2Sa 17:27–29). Thus the same man who had sheltered the last of Saul’s line also succoured David in the day of his affliction, showing a generous heart that honoured the LORD’s anointed whether high or low. Machir is to be distinguished from the elder Machir, the son of Manasseh. This Machir of Lo-debar stands as a quiet example of timely kindness to the people of God, a man whose open house and open hand ministered to both the helpless and the hunted.
webster_summary: A wealthy man of Lo-debar who sheltered Mephibosheth and supplied David at Mahanaim in his flight.

corruption_summary: A figure of Scripture, not a contested doctrine; his life is an example of timely kindness to the people of God.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the grace of timely kindness. Machir sheltered the helpless Mephibosheth and supplied the hunted David, ministering to the people of God in their need without thought of reward. The Scripture marks such hospitality with honour; he that gives a cup of cold water to the least of Christ’s shall not lose his reward.

Machir also shows a heart that honoured the LORD’s anointed in both his lowness and his exile. He cared for the last of Saul’s house and then for the fleeing David, asking nothing for himself. The believer is called to such generous and discerning love, ready to minister to the afflicted servants of God in whatever estate he finds them.

etymology: Hebrew Shobi, perhaps “one who turns back” or “captor,” an Ammonite who befriended David.
biblical_def: Shobi was the son of Nahash of Rabbah of the children of Ammon, who showed kindness to David in the day of his distress. When David fled before Absalom and came over the Jordan to Mahanaim, weary and hungry with the people that followed him, Shobi was one of three men who brought him relief, with Machir of Lo-debar and Barzillai the Gileadite; they brought beds and vessels, wheat and barley and flour, beans and lentils, honey and butter and cheese, for the king and his company in the wilderness (2Sa 17:27–29). It is striking that Shobi was an Ammonite, of the very royal house of Rabbah against which David had warred; yet he ministered to the fleeing king when many of David’s own people had turned to Absalom. His father Nahash had once shown David kindness, and Shobi, unlike his brother Hanun who insulted David’s messengers, repaid that bond with mercy. Shobi stands as a witness that the LORD raises up friends for His servants from unexpected quarters, even from among the nations, and that the kindness shown to the people of God is not forgotten across the generations.
webster_summary: An Ammonite of Rabbah, son of Nahash, who supplied David at Mahanaim during Absalom’s revolt.

corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the surprising friendship of Shobi. An Ammonite of the royal house, of a people often at war with Israel, he ministered to the fleeing David when many of David’s own had turned to Absalom. The LORD raises up help for His servants from unexpected quarters; the believer in his low estate may find kindness where he least looked for it.

Shobi’s mercy, set against his brother Hanun’s insolence, also shows that the bonds of kindness are honoured or broken by men, not by their nation. Nahash had once shown David kindness; Hanun spurned the bond, but Shobi kept it. Men of the same house may answer the same obligation in opposite ways, and the LORD takes notice of the one who shows mercy to His afflicted.

etymology: Hebrew Ittai, “with me” or “near,” a man of Gath, a Philistine city, who became a captain in David’s army.
biblical_def: Ittai the Gittite was a man of Gath, a Philistine by birth, who had come to dwell in Israel and cast in his lot with David. When David fled from Jerusalem before Absalom, he urged Ittai to return, saying, “thou art a stranger, and also an exile”; he had come but yesterday, and David would not have him share his uncertain wanderings (2Sa 15:19–20). But Ittai answered with one of the noblest confessions of loyalty in all Scripture: “As the LORD liveth, and as my lord the king liveth, surely in what place my lord the king shall be, whether in death or life, even there also will thy servant be” (2Sa 15:21). So Ittai passed over with the king, with all his men and their households. In the battle that followed, David set a third part of his army under the hand of Ittai, trusting the foreigner with the command of his troops (2Sa 18:2). Ittai the Gittite stands as a shining example of devoted, costly loyalty: a stranger who clave to the LORD’s anointed in the day of his rejection, choosing affliction with the true king over ease apart from him — a picture of faith that follows Christ whether in death or life.
webster_summary: A man of Gath who pledged undying loyalty to David in his flight and was given command of a third of his army.

corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the costly loyalty of Ittai. A stranger and exile, he might have returned to ease, but he chose to share the affliction of the rejected king, vowing to be with him in death or life. So the believer cleaves to Christ in the day of His reproach, counting it greater riches to suffer with the true King than to enjoy the world apart from Him.

Ittai, a Philistine of Gath received into the trust of David’s army, also displays the wideness of grace that gathers strangers into the people of God. The foreigner who clave to the LORD’s anointed was honoured above many of Israel who turned to Absalom. The kingdom of God is not bounded by blood; it is entered by faith that follows the King wherever He goes.

etymology: Hebrew Ira, “watchful” or “city,” a man of the family of Jair, a chief officer about David.
biblical_def: Ira the Jairite was a man of the family of Jair, named among the chief officers of David’s court in the list that closes the record of his reign: “And Ira also the Jairite was a chief ruler about David” (2Sa 20:26). The phrase rendered “chief ruler” is the same word used for priest, so that some understand Ira to have been a priest or chaplain unto David, a personal minister in things sacred about the king. He stands in the company of Zadok and Abiathar the priests, Benaiah over the guard, and the recorder and the scribe, in the roll of those who served the throne. Little else is told of Ira the Jairite, yet his place in the inspired record is not without weight: he was a trusted man near the person of the king, ministering perhaps in holy things in the royal household. He is to be distinguished from Ira the son of Ikkesh and Ira the Ithrite, who were among David’s mighty men. Ira the Jairite witnesses to the order of David’s court, in which place was made for the service of God beside the business of the kingdom, and a faithful man stood near the king to minister in sacred things.
webster_summary: A man of the family of Jair, a chief officer or priest about David’s person in his court.

The principle to recover is the order of David’s court, in which a man stood near the king to minister in sacred things. Place was made for the service of God beside the business of the kingdom; the throne of David did not divorce the holy from the affairs of state. A godly ruler keeps the worship of God near at hand, even in the midst of the cares of government.

Ira the Jairite, though little known, also reminds the reader that the LORD records the names of His faithful servants, however briefly they appear. The unnoticed minister near the king is named in the inspired roll; God forgets none who serve Him, and the obscure officer of David’s court is remembered in the Scripture that abides for ever.

etymology: Hebrew Achima’ats, perhaps “my brother is wrath” or “powerful,” the son of Zadok the priest.
biblical_def: Ahimaaz was the son of Zadok the priest, a swift and faithful young man who served David well in the days of Absalom’s revolt. When David fled Jerusalem, Ahimaaz and Jonathan the son of Abiathar stayed by En-rogel to carry tidings from the city to the king, and at great peril, hidden in a well at Bahurim, they brought David word of Ahithophel’s counsel so that he might cross the Jordan in time (2Sa 17:17–21). After the battle in which Absalom fell, Ahimaaz begged leave to run with the news, and being swift of foot he outran Cushi; the watchman knew him from afar, and the king said, “He is a good man, and cometh with good tidings” (2Sa 18:27). Yet Ahimaaz, in tender care for the king, would not be the one to tell him of his son’s death, but spoke only of the victory and let Cushi bear the heavy word. Ahimaaz stands as a model of faithful and swift service, a messenger eager to bear good news, and a man of gentle discretion who would not wound the king with grief he need not deliver. He is to be distinguished from Ahimaaz the father of Saul’s wife Ahinoam.
webster_summary: The son of Zadok the priest, a swift and faithful messenger who served David in Absalom’s revolt.

corruption_summary: A figure of Scripture, not a contested doctrine; he is a model of swift, faithful, and gentle service.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the eager faithfulness of Ahimaaz, who longed to run with good tidings and served the king at peril of his life. He is a small picture of the servant glad to bear the news of victory, like the feet that are beautiful upon the mountains that bring good tidings, that publish salvation (Isa 52:7). The believer should be as ready to carry the good news of God’s saving acts.

Ahimaaz also shows a tender discretion. Knowing the king’s love for Absalom, he would not be the one to bear the bitter word of his death, but spoke of the victory and left the heavy tidings to another. There is a wisdom in how truth is told; the faithful messenger weighs not only what is true but how a grieving heart may bear it, without ever speaking falsehood.

etymology: Hebrew Yehoshaphat, “the LORD hath judged,” the son of Ahilud, recorder under David and Solomon.
biblical_def: Jehoshaphat the son of Ahilud held the office of recorder, or remembrancer, in the courts of both David and Solomon. The recorder (in Hebrew the mazkir, “one who brings to remembrance”) was a high officer of state, keeper of the public records and chronicles of the kingdom, and a counsellor near the throne. He is named in the rolls of David’s chief officers alongside Joab over the host and the priests Zadok and Abiathar (2Sa 8:16; 20:24), and he continued in the same office under Solomon among the princes of that king’s court (1Ki 4:3). Through the changing of reigns Jehoshaphat kept his place, a steady and trusted servant who preserved the memory of the kingdom’s acts and affairs. He is to be distinguished from the later Jehoshaphat king of Judah. His name, “the LORD hath judged,” befits a keeper of records, for the writing down of a kingdom’s deeds is itself a kind of judgment, setting truth on record for the time to come. Jehoshaphat the recorder witnesses the value of faithful memory in the service of God and the state, and the honour of the man who keeps the record straight across the years.

corruption_summary: A figure of Scripture, not a contested doctrine; he witnesses the value of faithful memory in the service of God and state.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the honour of faithful memory. Jehoshaphat the recorder kept the chronicles of the kingdom across two reigns, preserving the truth of what was done for the time to come. The keeping of a true record is no small service; a people that forgets its history forgets the dealings of God with it, and a kingdom without faithful remembrance loses the wisdom of its past.

His name, “the LORD hath judged,” suits the office well, for the LORD Himself keeps a perfect record of all things, and a book of remembrance is written before Him for them that fear His name (Mal 3:16). The earthly recorder is a faint image of the heavenly; God forgets nothing, and the records of His servants’ lives stand sure before His throne.

etymology: Hebrew Serayah, “the LORD is prince” or “soldier of the LORD,” David’s royal scribe, called also Sheva, Shavsha, and Shisha.
biblical_def: Seraiah was the scribe, or royal secretary, in the court of David, named among the chief officers of the kingdom: “Zadok the son of Ahitub, and Ahimelech the son of Abiathar, were the priests; and Seraiah was the scribe” (2Sa 8:17). The same officer appears under several spellings of his name in the parallel records — Sheva (2Sa 20:25), Shavsha (1Ch 18:16), and Shisha (1Ki 4:3) — for the royal secretary of David, whose sons Elihoreph and Ahiah served Solomon as scribes after him. The scribe was a high officer of state, keeper of the king’s correspondence and the writing of his decrees, a man of learning and trust near the throne. He is to be distinguished from the later Seraiah, the chief priest carried away and slain when Jerusalem fell to Babylon. The name Seraiah, “the LORD is prince,” befits a servant of the king who is himself under the great King of all. Seraiah the scribe witnesses the place of learning and faithful writing in the service of God’s anointed, and the honour of the man who set the king’s words rightly in record.

corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the honour of the faithful scribe. Seraiah set the king’s words rightly in record and kept his correspondence, a man of learning trusted near the throne. The careful writing and preserving of words is a worthy service; the Scriptures themselves came to us through the labour of faithful scribes, and the LORD honours those who handle words with truth and diligence.

The several names borne by this one officer — Seraiah, Sheva, Shavsha, Shisha — remind the reader that the inspired record may give a man under different spellings without error, and that the harmony of the Scriptures is not broken by such variety. The careful student reconciles the parallel accounts rather than pitting them against each other; the word of God is consistent, and its apparent differences yield to patient and reverent study.

etymology: Hebrew Achishar, perhaps “my brother hath sung” or “brother of the prince,” the steward over Solomon’s household.
biblical_def: Ahishar was the officer set over the household of King Solomon, named among the great princes of that king’s court: “And Ahishar was over the household: and Adoniram the son of Abda was over the tribute” (1Ki 4:6). To be over the household was a high and trusted charge, the management of the king’s palace and all its affairs, the ordering of his servants and the care of his goods — an office like that which Joseph held in Pharaoh’s house and which Eliakim held in Hezekiah’s day, when the LORD said He would commit the key of the house of David to His servant’s shoulder (Isa 22:22). Ahishar appears but once, yet his single mention sets him among the chief men of Solomon’s glorious reign, when the kingdom was at its height in wealth and order. Little is told of him beyond his office, but that office speaks of great trust reposed in a faithful steward. Ahishar witnesses the honour of faithful stewardship in the house of the king, and the dignity of the servant set over much — a quiet reminder that the LORD looks for faithfulness in those entrusted with the care of His house and goods, that they may at last hear, “Well done, thou good and faithful servant.”

corruption_summary: A figure of Scripture, not a contested doctrine; he witnesses the honour of faithful stewardship in the house of the king.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the dignity of faithful stewardship. Ahishar was over the household of Solomon, entrusted with the care of the king’s house and goods. Such a charge calls for faithfulness above all; the steward must be found trustworthy in what is committed to him. The LORD looks for the same in His servants, that they may at last hear, “Well done, thou good and faithful servant; thou hast been faithful over a few things” (Matt 25:21).

The office of being over the household runs as a thread through Scripture — Joseph in Egypt, Eliakim in Judah — and points beyond itself to Christ, who is faithful as a Son over His own house, whose house are we (Heb 3:6). Ahishar, the steward of an earthly king, is a faint figure of the faithful steward of the house of God; and the believer is called to keep his lesser trust with the like fidelity.

etymology: Hebrew Elichoreph, perhaps “God of harvest” or “God is my reward,” one of the scribes of Solomon.
biblical_def: Elihoreph was one of the two scribes in the court of King Solomon, the sons of Shisha: “Elihoreph and Ahiah, the sons of Shisha, scribes; Jehoshaphat the son of Ahilud, the recorder” (1Ki 4:3). Their father Shisha had been the royal secretary of David, called also Seraiah, Sheva, and Shavsha; thus the office of scribe passed from father to sons, and the learning of the court was kept in a faithful house across the generations. As scribes, Elihoreph and his brother kept the king’s correspondence, drew up his decrees, and preserved the writings of the realm in the glorious days of Solomon’s reign, when wisdom and order filled the kingdom. Elihoreph is named but once, yet his place among the princes of Solomon witnesses the honour of his office and the continuance of faithful service in his family. His name, perhaps “God is my reward,” is fitting for a servant who labours not for himself but for his king and his God. Elihoreph stands as a quiet example of an inheritance of faithful service, a son carrying on the worthy work of his father in the house of the king.
webster_summary: One of the two scribes of Solomon, son of Shisha, continuing the office his father held under David.

corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the continuance of faithful service from father to sons. The scribe’s office passed from Shisha to Elihoreph and Ahiah, the learning and trust of the court kept in a faithful house across the generations. It is a good thing when godly diligence is handed down in a family, and children carry on the worthy work of their fathers in the service of God and the king.

Elihoreph, named but once among the princes of Solomon, also reminds the reader that the LORD records the obscure as well as the famous. The scribe whose deeds are not told is yet named in the inspired roll; God does not forget the quiet labourer in His service. The honour of a faithful man does not depend on the length of his record but on the truth of his work.

etymology: Hebrew Adoniram, “my lord is exalted,” the officer over the tribute and the levy; called also Adoram and Hadoram.
biblical_def: Adoniram, the son of Abda, was the officer set over the tribute, or the levy of forced labour, under David, Solomon, and Rehoboam. He is named in David’s court as Adoram over the tribute (2Sa 20:24), and in Solomon’s as Adoniram over the levy, in charge of the thirty thousand men raised to labour in Lebanon for the building of the temple (1Ki 4:6; 5:14). For long years he managed the great burden of the king’s works. But his office ended in violence: when the kingdom was divided and Rehoboam, refusing the people’s plea to lighten their yoke, sent Adoram to them, all Israel stoned him with stones that he died, and Rehoboam fled to Jerusalem (1Ki 12:18). Thus the man who had so long gathered the labour of the people became the object of their fury when a foolish king turned a heavy yoke heavier. Adoniram’s end witnesses the danger of a ruler who hardens his demands upon the people, and the bitter fruit of pride that will not hear wise counsel. His death was the first blow of the rebellion that tore ten tribes from the house of David, a sober monument to the cost of oppression and folly in the seat of power.

corruption_summary: A figure of Scripture, not a contested doctrine; his end witnesses the bitter fruit of oppression and folly in the seat of power.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the danger of a heavy yoke laid upon the people. Adoniram long managed the king’s levies, but when Rehoboam, spurning wise counsel, sent him to a people already provoked by his threat to make their yoke heavier, they stoned him to death. Rulers who harden their demands and will not hear the cry of the people sow the wind and reap the whirlwind; the seat of power is no shelter from the fruit of oppression.

Adoniram’s death was the first blow of the rebellion that tore ten tribes from the house of David, fulfilling the word of the LORD spoken by Ahijah the prophet. Even the folly of Rehoboam served the purpose of God, who had decreed the rending of the kingdom for Solomon’s idolatry. The LORD overrules the pride and folly of kings to accomplish His own righteous judgments, yet the guilt of the oppressor remains his own.
